D.treatment: reported knowing well what AI is
D.comparison: did not know what AI is

cells.quote: "approximately one-third of respondents (33.9%) indicated they did not know what artificial intelligence is, while 24.0% reported knowing well what AI is, and 42.0% indicated they roughly imagine what it is."
cells.note: The study text reports descriptive percentages from a secondary analysis of a national survey; it does not report an inferential test or manipulated treatment.

cells.quote: An unadjusted model produced an estimate of 0.33 [0.22 –0.43], while a model that included all cohort-speciﬁc confounders was nonidentiﬁed (i.e., no degrees of freedom, because of the small number of UK population-representative cohorts).
cells.note: Supplementary analysis of five cohorts designed to be representative of the wider UK population at inception (overall N = 50,306); the reported association is unadjusted.

cells.quote: Our meta-analysis included 29 studies ( N = 3765), that used rigorous pre-post designs, allowing us to make causal inferences about the effects of spatial training/instruction on mathematics performance. The results of this study were promising, with an overall effect size of 0.28 (Hedges ’s g) for spatial training on mathematics compared to controls 9.
cells.note: Pooled result from the cited meta-analysis of spatial training studies.

cells.quote: Larger gains were found for training based on concrete materials (e.g., physical 3D shapes, manipulatives, blocks) compared to computer-based training.
cells.note: Moderator contrast reported within the cited meta-analysis; no separate effect size is printed.

cells.quote: Based on an analysis of 206 training studies across a 25-year period they reported that spatial interventions led to an average effect size (Hedges’s g) of 0.47 (half a standard deviation) for training groups relative to controls 4.
cells.note: Pooled result from the cited 2013 meta-analysis.

cells.quote: Students from many countries, including the UK and US, show relative weaknesses in shape and space domains on international assessments of mathematics (e.g., PISA and TIMMS) compared to other mathematics sub-domains 16 suggesting that spatial instruction should be increased rather than eliminated.
cells.note: The commentary reports this cited assessment comparison but does not state the underlying design or a numerical effect size.
